title: Testing a Mineral
objective: After this level you can identify a mineral by its hardness, streak and luster, using the Mohs scale.
summary: Geologists identify minerals by hardness on the Mohs scale (talc 1 to diamond 10), by streak (the color of the powder) and by luster (how the surface shines).

cards.headline: Fool's gold fooled prospectors. A plain white tile would have saved them.
cards.body: Pyrite has gold's color and a metal's shine. Color and shine can lie, so geologists test minerals in ways that are much harder to fool.

cards.headline: The scratch test
cards.body: In 1812, the German mineralogist Friedrich Mohs ranked ten minerals by hardness, from soft talc at 1 to diamond at 10. The rule is simple: a harder mineral scratches a softer one. Glass rates about 5.5, so quartz, at 7, scratches a window. Your fingernail rates a little over 2: it can scratch talc and gypsum, but not calcite.
cards.callout: Talc 1 · Gypsum 2 · Calcite 3 · Fluorite 4 · Apatite 5 · Orthoclase 6 · Quartz 7 · Topaz 8 · Corundum 9 · Diamond 10

cards.fact: The step from 9 to 10 on the Mohs scale is far bigger than the step from 3 to 4.
cards.context: Fluorite (4) is only about 25% harder than calcite (3), but diamond (10) is more than 300% harder than corundum (9). The scale puts minerals in order; it doesn't space them evenly. It tells you who scratches whom, not by how much.

cards.headline: Streak: a mineral's true colors
cards.body: A mineral's color can vary a lot. The color of its powder, called its streak, is far more consistent. To see it, scrape the mineral across a streak plate of unglazed porcelain. Hematite can look black or silver, yet it always leaves a reddish streak; its name comes from the Greek for blood. Pyrite leaves a greenish-black streak. Real gold leaves a yellow one.

cards.headline: Luster: how it shines
cards.body: Luster describes how a mineral's surface reflects light. Opaque minerals like pyrite and galena have a metallic luster: they shine like metal. Quartz has a vitreous luster, a fancy word for glassy. Hardness, streak and luster together shrink the suspect list fast.

cards.headline: Mineral tests: passed
learned: Mohs ranks hardness from talc 1 to diamond 10
The scale is an order, not even steps
Streak is the color of the powder
Luster is how a mineral shines

questions.prompt: The mineral at the top of the Mohs scale, at 10, is _____.

options.label: corundum
options.rationale: Corundum rates 9, one step below the top.

questions.explanation: Mohs ranked ten minerals from talc (1) to diamond (10).

questions.prompt: Why do geologists trust a mineral's streak more than its color?

options.label: Its powder color varies far less
The streak measures the mineral's hardness
options.rationale: Hardness comes from the scratch test.

options.label: The plate makes every mineral shine
options.rationale: Shine is luster, a separate clue.

options.label: Color only works on metallic minerals
options.rationale: Color varies for many minerals, metallic or not.

questions.explanation: A mineral's apparent color can vary a lot, but the color of its powder is far more consistent.

questions.prompt: Put these minerals in order on the Mohs scale, from softest to hardest.
questions.explanation: Talc (1), calcite (3), fluorite (4), quartz (7), diamond (10). A harder mineral scratches a softer one.
